questions.q: Identify the question type: "What was the author's mother's reaction when she saw the author imitating Mumtaz Ali's dance at age seven?" Is this literal or inferential?
questions.a: Literal. The text explicitly states: "my mother, who was quietly watching, was the one who said, 'Kumudini, you are born to dance.'" A wrong answer (inferential) reveals the student cannot distinguish between directly stated information and implied meaning, often because they overcomplicate straightforward retrieval questions.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the author says "I find this assertion dubious" about dancers who claim they were "born to dance". What textual evidence supports her skepticism?
questions.a: The author calls the assertion dubious because her own experience contradicts it: she was forced into dance by her mother, did not enjoy it initially ("they were no fun"), and had to struggle to understand the movements. A wrong answer reveals the student confuses the author's adult reflection with the childhood experience, or misses the contrast between the romanticized "born to dance" narrative and the author's grueling reality.

questions.q: Apply the literal/inferential distinction: The text says "Discipline in one's daily routine does bring discipline in thinking." Formulate one literal question and one inferential question based on this sentence.
questions.a: Literal: What does the author say brings discipline in thinking? (Answer: Discipline in one's daily routine). Inferential: How might the British school discipline have influenced the author's later choreographic work? (Requires connecting "neat little piles" of thoughts to structured choreography). A wrong answer shows inability to generate questions at different cognitive levels, often producing two literal or two inferential questions.

questions.q: Analyze the author's reaction to her mother's death: "I did not know where to turn or what to do with my hands, which hung loose from my body. Then suddenly they clutched my stomach. Hunger pangs? I hadn't eaten for three days..." What does this physical description infer about her psychological state, and which two textual details support this inference?
questions.a: The description infers emotional numbness and dislocation masking deep grief. Evidence 1: "The air was still and nobody looked at me" (social isolation). Evidence 2: "I was afraid of appearing greedy, so I underplayed my emotions" (suppressed expression). A wrong answer treats the hunger as purely physical, missing the metaphorical "emptiness I wanted to fill" that the author later connects to her choreography.

questions.q: Evaluate this student inference: "The author's grandmother was completely wrong about women's modesty because the author became a successful dancer." Is this a valid text-based inference? Why or why not?
questions.a: Invalid. The text shows the author challenging her grandmother ("What about the short blouses you wear...?"), but also acknowledges "My grandmother, of course, was not completely to blame... It is a problem that goes deep into the texture of our society." A valid inference must account for the author's nuanced critique, not a simplistic right/wrong judgment. A wrong answer reveals the student imposes personal opinion instead of tracking the author's evolving perspective.

questions.q: Create an inferential question about the author's time in post-war Germany that requires connecting the external environment to her internal artistic growth. Provide the textual evidence a good answer would use.
questions.a: Question: "How did the author's observation of hungry children in Germany differ from her experience in India, and what did this teach her about context in choreography?" Evidence: "Hungry children begging for food is a common sight in India, yet, in Germany the same sight created a different sensation" and "One changes the placement of a choreographic piece on stage and it looks quite different. I myself was a changed person when placed in different surroundings." A poor answer creates a literal question (e.g., "Where did she tour?") or an inference unsupported by the Germany passage.
